title: National Zoo Celebrates Three New Red Panda Cubs
summary:
This International Red Panda Day, the Smithsonian's National Zoo has three small reasons to celebrate. Three red panda cubs were born earlier this summer at the zoo's conservation campus in Front Royal, Virginia.

On May 29, a 3-year-old female named Sequoia and a 12-year-old male named Mow Mow welcomed twins — one female, one male. On June 11, a 3-year-old female named Keahi gave birth to a single female, sired by a 7-year-old male named Rocket.

"The new cubs are ensuring the population overall," Jessica Kordell, assistant curator of carnivores, told Popular Science. "We can't conserve the species and continue to breed them if we don't have the animals."

The cubs have spent the summer in nest boxes with their parents, drinking milk and sleeping. Staff have started placing bamboo inside, though the cubs haven't eaten it yet. They're becoming more mobile, and their personalities are emerging.

"The singleton... is definitely feisty and huff-quacks at us every chance she gets," Kordell said. "The twins are a bit more quiet and shy. They have each other and they rely on that."

Red pandas are endangered mammals found in the treetops of Nepal, India, Bhutan, Myanmar, and China. They're most closely related to raccoons. They eat mostly bamboo — two to four pounds a day — but digest only about 24 percent of it, so they must eat 20 to 30 percent of their body weight daily.

Their reddish fur matches lichen growing on trees, Kordell noted, while their black bellies blend into shadows. In cold weather, red pandas enter "torpor" — a deep sleep that lowers their body temperature and saves energy.

Fewer than 10,000 remain in the wild, and habitat loss is the main threat. In Nepal, their habitat has fragmented into 400 small forest patches. The Red Panda Network has worked since 2007 on community-based conservation.

These cubs matter because they pass their parents' genetic material to the next generation — a crucial step for a species in trouble.
why_it_matters: Zoo births are one line of defence for a species whose real problem is habitat: with fewer than 10,000 red pandas left and forests split into tiny patches, the survival of the species depends on whether conservation money and political attention go to protecting Himalayan forests, not just to breeding animals in enclosures.

background_read: Red pandas were described by scientists in the 1820s, decades before the giant panda was known to the West — which is why the black-and-white bear later had to be called the GIANT panda. For a long time people assumed red pandas were close relatives of raccoons or bears; genetic studies eventually placed them in their own family, Ailuridae, with no close living relatives.

Today red pandas are listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (the world's official inventory of species at risk of extinction). Their numbers have fallen sharply as forests in the eastern Himalayas are cut for farmland, roads and firewood. The Red Panda Network (a conservation charity that works with local communities in Nepal) has run community-based programmes since 2007, training and paying local people to guard and monitor forests.

The cubs at the Smithsonian's National Zoo (a major zoo in Washington, D.C., run by the Smithsonian Institution) belong to a cooperative global breeding plan in which zoos swap animals and share records to keep captive populations genetically healthy. Because red pandas are solitary and easily stressed in the wild, keepers usually let mothers raise cubs in quiet nest boxes rather than hand-rearing them. Each surviving cub is a small insurance policy against extinction.

perspectives.description: Each cub adds new genetic material to a captive population that could one day help restock the wild. Zoos also fund research on diet, disease and reproduction that field biologists cannot easily collect, and they introduce millions of visitors to a species most will never see in a forest.

Critics argue that zoo births can create a comforting illusion of progress while the actual habitat keeps shrinking into 400 fragmented patches in Nepal alone. They say money and effort spent on captive breeding would protect more animals if it went directly to forests, anti-poaching patrols and local livelihoods.

Captive breeding and community-based conservation solve different problems and are usually treated as complements rather than rivals. The Red Panda Network's work since 2007 targets the cause of decline, while zoos maintain a safety-net population and genetic records that would be lost if wild numbers crashed further.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — what happens to these cubs
perspectives.description: The cubs will eventually be matched with mates at other zoos under international breeding plans, and cubs of the shy twins may carry genes not yet represented elsewhere. Whether that matters in the long run depends on whether Himalayan forests are still connected and cool enough by the time their descendants could be released.
